cards.front: Describe the waterfall model of software development.
cards.back: A linear sequence of stages - requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance - in which each stage is completed and signed off before the next one starts.

keyPoints.text: each stage finished before the next begins

mcq.correct: A linear sequence of stages - requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance - in which each stage is completed and signed off before the next one starts.
distractors: Development proceeds in short iterations that each deliver working software
Requirements are allowed to change throughout the build
Testing runs continuously in parallel with implementation

cards.explanation: Those three options all describe iterative or Agile approaches, which is the point of contrasting them with waterfall.

cards.front: State one advantage and one disadvantage of the waterfall model.
cards.back: Advantage: the stages and their documentation are clear, so the project is easy to plan and manage when the requirements are stable. Disadvantage: it copes badly with change, because working software appears only at the end and a requirement error found in testing is expensive to fix.

synonyms: working software only at the end

cards.explanation: The model is not wrong, just suited to projects where the requirements genuinely will not change, such as safety-critical systems.

cards.front: What is the essential idea behind Agile development?
cards.back: Delivering working software in short iterations, welcoming changing requirements even late in development, and using continuous feedback from the customer rather than a fixed plan agreed at the start.
cards.explanation: Agile trades the detailed up-front planning of waterfall for the ability to respond to change.

cards.back: An approach that builds a system quickly through prototyping, reusing existing components and involving users throughout, accepting some loss of documentation or refinement in exchange for speed of delivery.
cards.explanation: RAD suits projects where the requirement is best discovered by showing the user something that works.

cards.front: Why is testing not the same thing as debugging?
cards.back: Testing is running a program with chosen inputs to find defects and check it meets its requirements. Debugging is locating the cause of a defect that testing has revealed and fixing it.

mcq.correct: Testing is running a program with chosen inputs to find defects and check it meets its requirements. Debugging is locating the cause of a defect that testing has revealed and fixing it.
distractors: Testing removes errors while debugging only reports them
Debugging happens before testing
They are two names for the same activity

cards.explanation: Testing can show that errors exist but never that they do not; debugging is the repair work that follows.

cards.front: Name three practices associated with Extreme Programming.
cards.back: Pair programming, test-driven development and continuous integration; short release cycles with on-site customer involvement are also central.

mcq.correct: Pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration
distractors: Waterfall stages, sign-off documents and a fixed scope
Prototyping, user feedback and scrum meetings only
Code review, release planning and a Gantt chart

cards.explanation: XP is an Agile framework, so its practices all serve short feedback cycles: tests written first, two people on every piece of code, and integration several times a day so that faults surface while they are small. A fixed scope with formal sign-off is the opposite philosophy and belongs to waterfall.

cards.front: What is the difference between iterative and incremental development?
cards.back: Iterative development repeats the cycle of build, test and refine to improve the same functionality; incremental development builds the system in separate finished pieces, adding new functionality each time.

keyPoints.text: iterative repeats and refines the same work

mcq.correct: Iterative refines the same work; incremental adds new finished pieces
distractors: Iterative adds new pieces; incremental refines existing ones
They are synonyms with no distinction
Iterative is waterfall and incremental is Agile

cards.explanation: A sketch redrawn three times to get it right is iterative; drawing the outline, then adding colour, then adding detail is incremental. Most Agile methods do both at once, which is why the words are used loosely - but an exam question asking for the distinction wants exactly this difference.

cards.front: Distinguish unit, integration, system and acceptance testing.
cards.back: Unit tests one module in isolation, integration tests how modules work together, system tests the whole finished program against its specification, and acceptance testing is done by the client to decide whether the system is fit for use.

keyPoints.text: system: the whole program against the specification
acceptance: by the client, to decide fitness for use

mcq.correct: Module alone, modules together, whole system, client sign-off
distractors: Whole system first, then modules, then integration, then client
All four test the same thing at different speeds
Unit and system are the same; integration and acceptance are the same

cards.explanation: The order matters because faults are cheapest to find early: a unit test that fails points at one function, whereas the same fault found in system testing could be anywhere. Acceptance testing is also the only one of the four usually carried out by people who did not write the code.

cards.front: What is the difference between white box and black box testing?
cards.back: White box testing uses knowledge of the internal code to design tests that cover paths and branches; black box testing uses only the specification, choosing inputs from what the program is supposed to do.

keyPoints.text: white box uses the internal code
black box uses only the specification

synonyms: each can miss what the other catches

mcq.correct: White box uses the code; black box uses only the specification
distractors: White box is automated; black box is manual
White box tests the interface; black box tests the internals
White box is done by the client; black box by the developer

cards.explanation: A black box test cannot detect code that is never reachable, and a white box test cannot detect a feature that was never written, since it only checks what exists. That is why both are used. Statement and branch coverage are white box measures; equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis are black box techniques.

cards.front: A program accepts an integer age from 18 to 65 inclusive. Give one item each of valid, invalid and boundary test data.
cards.back: Valid: 40. Invalid: 17 or 100, and a non-numeric entry such as 'abc'. Boundary: 17, 18, 65 and 66.

keyPoints.text: a valid value inside the range
boundary values just inside and just outside each end

distractors: Valid 18; invalid 65; boundary 40
Valid 40; invalid 41; boundary 18 only
Valid 65; invalid 66; boundary 18 and 65 only

cards.explanation: Boundary values are where off-by-one faults live, which is why the pair either side of each limit is tested rather than the limits alone. Testing 18 and 65 by themselves would miss a program that wrongly uses `<` instead of `<=`. Invalid data should include the wrong type as well as the wrong value.

cards.front: Give two reasons why waterfall suits a safety-critical system better than Agile.
cards.back: The requirements are fixed and fully known before work starts, and the formal documentation and sign-off at each stage provide the audit trail that certification requires.

keyPoints.text: requirements are fixed and known in advance
documentation and sign-off give an audit trail

mcq.correct: Fixed requirements, and formal documentation for certification
distractors: It is faster to build and needs fewer staff
It allows requirements to change late, which is safer
It needs no testing, because each stage is signed off

cards.explanation: Certifying an aircraft control system needs evidence of what was specified, what was built and what was tested, which waterfall's stage documents supply naturally. Its weakness - that changes are expensive - is not a weakness when the requirements genuinely will not move. Testing is still required at every stage; sign-off does not replace it.

cards.front: What is a dry run, and what does a trace table record?
cards.back: A dry run is working through an algorithm by hand on paper with sample data. A trace table records the value of each variable after every step, alongside the output produced.

keyPoints.text: working through the algorithm by hand with sample data
the trace table records each variable's value at each step
it also records output and any conditions tested

mcq.correct: Manual simulation on paper; the table records each variable per step
distractors: Running the program under a debugger; the table records memory addresses
A test done by the client; the table records user actions
An automated test; the table records execution time

cards.explanation: A trace table exposes loop faults that reading the code hides, because the faulty iteration is written down rather than imagined. Its limits are worth stating too: it only exercises the data chosen, so it can confirm a fault but never prove its absence - which is what separates a dry run from a proof of correctness.
